hypothesis: PI(16:0/18:2(9Z,12Z)) is increased or characteristic in 12-month-old infants receiving dairy-based complementary protein relative to meat-based complementary protein.
rationale: Searches located no primary study reporting PI(16:0/18:2) (LMGP06010959) — or phosphatidylinositol species generally — as elevated in dairy-fed versus meat-fed infants at any complementary-feeding timepoint. The most directly relevant literature is the U.S. formula-fed infant randomized controlled feeding trial (meat- vs. dairy-based complementary foods, 5–12 months, Denver cohort) whose serum metabolomics paper explicitly concluded that protein source (meat vs. dairy) did not differentially impact serum metabolites, and whose companion microbiome/metabolome network-learning analysis emphasized age rather than protein source as the dominant driver; neither result surfaced PI(16:0/18:2) as a dairy-associated feature. What can be found is only generic, compositional/pathway-level reasoning: dairy fat, and specifically the milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) and buttermilk-derived polar lipid fractions used in dairy foods and formulas, contain phosphatidylinositol as a minor phospholipid class (~5–10% of MFGM PL), and PI species with 16:0 and 18:2 acyl chains are catalogued in milk/buttermilk lipidomes. That makes a dairy-driven increase in a PI species biologically plausible but entirely untested for this feature+group combination. Countervailing considerations further weaken the specific direction: (i) meat (muscle tissue) is itself a rich source of membrane glycerophospholipids including PI, so a dairy>meat direction is not compositionally obvious; (ii) in human milk the dominant PI species reported by lipidomic profiling is PI(18:0/18:2) rather than PI(16:0/18:2); and (iii) both arms of this type of trial typically continue the same infant formula, compressing any dairy-lipid contrast. Per the rubric, relevant material was found but it is generic/theoretical rather than feature- and group-specific, and no study points the opposite way for this exact feature, so the score is 1 (Weak) rather than 0 or -1.

evidence.title: Different Blood Metabolomics Profiles in Infants Consuming a Meat- or Dairy-Based Complementary Diet
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed term infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial consuming meat- vs. dairy-based complementary foods from 5 to 12 months, followed to 24 months
evidence.relevance: Most directly matched study population and exposure contrast (dairy vs. meat complementary protein at 12 months). Targeted/untargeted serum metabolomics reported that protein-food source did not differentially impact serum metabolites; no phosphatidylinositol species such as PI(16:0/18:2) was highlighted as dairy-characteristic, so it provides no support for the hypothesized direction.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age and diet on the gut microbial and metabolomic environment of U.S. infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed infants, 5–12 months, randomized to meat vs. dairy complementary protein; fecal metagenomics and metabolomics
evidence.relevance: Same trial, fecal microbiome/metabolome readout closest to the present study design. The available text frames age as the principal driver of the microbial/metabolomic environment and does not name PI(16:0/18:2) or phosphatidylinositols as dairy-group markers.

evidence.title: Different gut microbiota in U.S. formula-fed infants consuming a meat vs. dairy-based complementary foods: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed infants 5–12 months randomized to meat- or dairy-based complementary foods
evidence.relevance: Companion report from the same trial focused on gut microbiota and fecal SCFAs; documents the dairy vs. meat exposure contrast at 12 months but reports no lipid/phosphatidylinositol metabolite findings, confirming absence of direct evidence for this feature.

evidence.title: Digestion and Absorption of Milk Phospholipids in Newborns and Adults
evidence.study_population: Review of human newborns and adults; milk phospholipid digestion physiology
evidence.relevance: Indirect/compositional support: documents that the milk fat globule membrane contains phosphatidylinositol along with SM, PC, PE and PS, establishing dairy foods as a dietary source of PI species that could plausibly reach the infant gut lumen — but pathway-level only, with no data on PI(16:0/18:2) or on dairy vs. meat complementary feeding.

evidence.title: Fatty acid composition and phospholipid types used in infant formulas modifies the establishment of human gut bacteria in germ-free mice
evidence.study_population: Germ-free mice colonized with human infant gut bacteria; infant formula phospholipid sources (milk MFGM vs. soy lecithin)
evidence.relevance: Indirect animal-model evidence that dietary phospholipid source alters gut microbial establishment, and states PI comprises roughly 5–10% of human MFGM phospholipids; supports plausibility of a dairy-lipid-driven PI signal in the gut but does not test PI(16:0/18:2) or the dairy vs. meat infant contrast.

evidence.title: Profile of Human Milk Phospholipids at Different Lactation Stages with UPLC/Q-TOF-MS: Characterization, Distribution, and Differences
evidence.study_population: Human milk samples across lactation stages (lipidomic profiling)
evidence.relevance: Provides the milk PI molecular-species context: PI(18:0/18:2), not PI(16:0/18:2), is reported as the most abundant PI species in human milk, tempering the assumption that PI(16:0/18:2) is a distinctive dairy-diet marker.

evidence.title: In-Depth Lipidomic Analysis of Molecular Species of Triacylglycerides, Diacylglycerides, Glycerophospholipids, and Sphingolipids of Buttermilk by GC-MS/FID, HPLC-ELSD, and UPLC-QToF-MS
evidence.relevance: Confirms that dairy-derived polar lipid fractions contain numerous PI molecular species, i.e., a dairy dietary source exists for PI lipids; purely compositional food-chemistry evidence, not infant outcome data.

evidence.title: LIPID MAPS LMSD record LMGP06010959 — PI(16:0_18:2)
evidence.relevance: Confirms the identity/formula (C43H79O13P, exact mass 834.5258) of the queried feature so that literature searches were anchored to the correct lipid species.

contradicting_evidence: No study was found reporting PI(16:0/18:2) as higher in meat-fed than dairy-fed infants, so there is no directly opposite finding. However, the single most relevant human trial (serum metabolomics from the 5–12 month meat vs. dairy randomized feeding trial) reported a null result — protein source did not differentially affect the serum metabolome — which fails to support the hypothesized dairy enrichment. Additionally, muscle/meat tissue is itself phospholipid-rich (including PI), and human-milk lipidomics identifies PI(18:0/18:2) rather than PI(16:0/18:2) as the dominant PI species, both of which weaken the compositional argument for a dairy>meat direction.

caveats: Untargeted lipidomic annotations at this level (exact sn-position PI(16:0/18:2(9Z,12Z))) are typically MS1/level-2 confidence and may not be distinguishable from isobaric PI 34:2 isomers, so cross-study matching is uncertain. Sample matrix matters: if this feature was measured in stool, luminal PI reflects both diet-derived and host/mucosal/microbial membrane lipid turnover, and PI is largely hydrolyzed by pancreatic phospholipase A2 before the colon, so a direct dietary-dairy-to-fecal-PI link is not guaranteed. Both arms of the reference trial received the same infant formula, which dilutes the dairy-fat contrast. My final three planned queries (beef/muscle PI species and additional milk PI species profiling) could not be executed because the search quota was exhausted, so evidence on the meat-side PI contribution is incomplete. Absence of published evidence here is not evidence of absence — this may simply be an unstudied feature.
